- **Paper: "ChatGPT's Ontological Landscape" (William L. Benzon, Nov. 2023 working paper)**
  - Explores how ChatGPT organizes and navigates "ontological" category structure — physical vs. living vs. animal vs. human capacities (the Aristotelian/Great Chain of Being hierarchy)
  - Also examines the concrete/abstract distinction, using the salt vs. NaCl example: same physical referent, but embedded in different conceptual systems (common-sense vs. scientific)
  - Section 1 ("From Salt and NaCl to the Great Chain") quizzes ChatGPT on salt/NaCl, Morning Star/Evening Star (intension vs. extension), the Great Chain of Being, Aristotle's *De Anima* (vegetative/sensitive/rational souls), and Plato's charioteer parable
  - Section 2 ("Mapping ChatGPT's ontological landscape") probes concrete vs. abstract questions and uses Waddington's epigenetic landscape as a metaphor for how ChatGPT settles into conceptual categories
  - Section 3 ("ChatGPT Plays 20 Questions") has ChatGPT play the game as guesser against six targets (bicycle, squid, justice, apple, evolution, truth), twice each
    - Finding: ChatGPT generally needed fewer questions/hints to guess abstract targets (e.g. justice, evolution) than concrete ones (e.g. bicycle, apple), suggesting it may navigate abstract conceptual space more efficiently
    - Truth was an outlier, requiring many hints despite being abstract
    - Paper is explicit that the sample size is far too small to support any real statistical claim
  - Appendix lists related papers on cognitive ontology and cultural evolution of conceptual systems
- **Student's sidenote (Qi An)**
  - Notes the original presentation slides were lost, so the sidenote reconstructs the talk's main points from memory
  - Point 1 — "give me 20 things, anything": prompting ChatGPT with a seed pattern ("butterfly, dragonfly, ...") caused it to keep the "-fly" pattern until exhausted, then drift to flying bugs, then general bugs, then flying mammals; asking for "50 more" caused further collapse into general mammals
  - Point 2 — 20 Questions experiment:
    - Hypothesis: ChatGPT's first question is often abstract-vs-concrete, and since English has fewer abstract words, guessing abstract targets takes fewer steps
    - Related takeaway: an A-or-B question tends to favor whichever option is less frequent in the vocabulary
    - Identified issue: the concrete/abstract word ratio used in the informal test didn't match the real distribution in the English dictionary
    - Proposed fix: sample an equal number of concrete and abstract words from a curated dictionary, tell ChatGPT the keyword was drawn from that fixed list, then rerun the game
    - Result of the corrected experiment: no significant bias toward either category
